newsitem.title: INDIA: Overseas money seen driving Indian stocks rally.
newsitem.headline: Overseas money seen driving Indian stocks rally.

text.p: Strong foreign portfolio inflows and hopes of an economic upturn are expected to sustain a bull run in Indian stocks this week, fund managers said.
They said diversion of profits from a buoyant Wall Street into emerging markets would propel local shares to greater heights after the Indian market hit 33-month highs last week.
"Well, the theory is that people have made lot of gains in U.S. markets and are sitting on profits they really want to cash on," Narendra Nagpal, research head at BZW Ltd told Reuters.
"Among the attractive destinationS in emerging markets, India is a strong bet with the economy turning around."

Falling interest rates, increased liquidity and a drop in individual taxes introduced in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget are expected to spur a limping economy, though data so far have not indicated an economic upturn.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share index surged 190.58 points, or 4.6 percent, to 4,323.82 last week, extending the winning streak to the sixth week in a row.
Analysts expect the rally to take the index past its all-time peak of 4,643.31 reached on September 12, 1994.

S.M. Athalye, associate vice president (investments) at Tata Asset Management Ltd says U.S. funds are shifting a portion of the profits from buoyant Wall Street to emerging markets -- and India was getting a trickle of these inflows which in local terms seem huge.
The Dow Jones Industrials jumped 208 points to close at a record 7,895.81 last week after a smaller-than-expected rise in U.S. June payrolls confirming moderating growth amid low inflation.
U.S. stocks have soared nearly 22 percent in 1997 helped by strong corporate earnings growth and robust economic indicators, analysts said.
"There are new funds entering the market (Indian). That's a good sign," said Ajay Srinivasan, chief investment officer at ITC-Threadneedle Asset Management Ltd.
Official figures show that net investments by foreign institutional investors (FIIs) in India have been on the rise, totalling $365.5 million in June against $198.4 million in May.
"If you got a global fund manager and he's done very well in U.S. markets, he's going to look pretty overweight in the U.S.," Nikhil Khattau, chief executive at Sun F&C told Reuters.
"So, he'll want to reallocate some of that portfolio probably into emerging markets as a hedge if nothing else. So, as a result you'll see flows to a certain extent."

Despite the 40 percent surge seen in the Bombay index this year, money was flowing only into top-quality stocks which enjoyed good earnings growth, low price multiples and good liquidity, analysts said.
"Quality companies with sustainable businesses and transparent management...these companies are performing well," Khattau said.
"The market is realising that there is a premium to be paid for quality and that's what we are seeing," he said.

Indian companies earnings are forecast to growth by about 20-25 percent in 1997/98 (April-March) helped by lower interest rates and easier money conditions against flat growth last year when operations were hit by tight liquidity and slack demand.
"We expect earnings growth of about 20 percent in 1997/98. India has attractive valuations and money will always flow into borders where returns are high," BZW's Nagpal said.
